hardy-weinberg-s1.title: Genotype counts in three plant populations
hardy-weinberg-s1.text: A wildflower species has a gene with two codominant alleles, A and a, so every genotype can be identified from the plants' flower-pigment pattern. Researchers counted 500 flowering adults in each of three populations. Population X grows in a large meadow and is pollinated by bees. Population Y grows on a cliff where bees are rare, and most of its seeds come from flowers that pollinated themselves. Population Z grows on soil where, in seedling surveys, AA and aa seedlings were seen to die more often than Aa seedlings.

table.caption: Observed numbers of each genotype among 500 adults per population

hardy-weinberg-s2.title: Frequency of a recessive allele in four laboratory populations
hardy-weinberg-s2.text: Researchers founded four populations of flour beetles from one stock in which the frequency (q) of a recessive allele, a, was 0.50. Beetles with genotype aa have a reddish body; AA and Aa beetles look the same. Each population was treated differently for 20 generations. Population 1: 2,000 breeding adults, nothing else done. Population 2: 2,000 breeding adults, but every reddish (aa) beetle was removed before it could breed. Population 3: 2,000 breeding adults, but each generation 10% of the breeders were replaced by beetles from a stock in which q = 0.10. Population 4: 10 breeding adults chosen at random each generation.

items.q: Calculate p, the frequency of allele A, in population Y. Give your answer to two decimal places.
If population Y were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with the allele frequencies it has, how many of its 500 plants would be expected to be Aa? Give a whole number.

why.correct: p = 0.64, q = 0.36. Expected Aa = 2pq × 500 = 2 × 0.64 × 0.36 × 500 = 230.4, about 230 plants. Only 40 were observed.

items.q: Which population's genotype counts are closest to Hardy-Weinberg expectations?
options: Population X
Population Y
Population Z
The three are equally close, since each has 500 plants

why.correct: X: p = (636 + 164) ÷ 1,000 = 0.80. Expected 320 AA, 160 Aa, 20 aa; observed 318, 164, 18. χ² = 0.01 + 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.31, far below any critical value.
options: Correct: observed counts are within a few plants of the expected 320, 160 and 20.
Y has 40 heterozygotes where about 230 are expected: a large deficit.
Z: p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, so 240 Aa are expected, but 300 were seen: an excess.
Sample size does not decide fit; the counts in Y and Z are far from expected.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the genotype counts in population Y?
options: Selfing pairs like alleles, so homozygotes rise and heterozygotes fall while p and q stay the same.
Natural selection against heterozygotes removes Aa plants, which lowers the frequency of allele a in each generation.
Gene flow from bee-pollinated populations brings in extra AA and aa plants, so the cliff plants become homozygous.
The small cliff population has nearly lost allele a by genetic drift, so few of its plants can be heterozygous.

why.correct: Self-fertilization is extreme nonrandom mating. Each selfing halves the share of heterozygotes among the offspring, so homozygotes pile up while p and q stay the same.
options: Correct: the deficit of heterozygotes matches the mating system described.
The stimulus describes self-pollination, not selection; nothing shows that Aa plants die more often.
Bees are rare on the cliff, so pollen from bee-pollinated populations is unlikely to arrive; gene flow would not raise homozygosity anyway.
Allele a is not lost: q = 0.36, which would give about 230 heterozygotes under random mating.

items.q: In population Z, p = 0.60 and q = 0.40. Which statement best explains its genotype counts?
options: Aa seedlings survive better than either homozygote, leaving more adult heterozygotes than 2pq predicts.
Plants in Z mate with relatives, which produces more heterozygotes than random mating would.
Allele A is dominant, so it pairs with allele a more often than chance and creates extra heterozygotes.
Population Z is in equilibrium, because its two allele frequencies add up to exactly 1 as they should.

why.correct: Expected among adults: 180 AA, 240 Aa, 80 aa. Observed: 150, 300, 50. Selection among seedlings, which removes more AA and aa than Aa, leaves a surplus of heterozygotes among the adults counted.
options: Correct: selection between seed and adult distorts the adult genotype counts.
Mating with relatives produces fewer heterozygotes, not more.
The alleles are codominant here, and dominance does not change how gametes combine anyway.
p + q always equals 1; equilibrium is judged by whether genotype counts match p², 2pq, q², and they do not.

items.q: Which population's results are consistent with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene?
options: Population 1
Population 2
Population 3
Population 4

why.correct: Population 1 is large, closed, not selected and mating at random, and q stays at 0.49-0.51 for 20 generations.
options: Correct: q holds steady at about 0.50.
q falls from 0.50 to 0.05 because aa beetles are removed: selection.
q falls toward 0.10, the frequency in the stock supplying replacement beetles: gene flow.
q wanders between 0.40 and 0.80 at random: drift in a population of 10.

items.q: In population 2, q fell by 0.25 in the first two generations but by less than 0.05 in the last ten. Which explanation best accounts for the slowdown?
options: As q falls, nearly all a alleles sit in Aa beetles, which look normal and are not removed.
The beetles adapted to the removal of aa beetles by producing fewer aa offspring each generation.
The researchers removed fewer reddish beetles in later generations because there were more beetles overall.
Mutation from A to a speeds up when q is low, adding back the a alleles removed by selection.

why.correct: Only aa beetles are removed, and they make up q² of the population. At q = 0.5, a quarter of beetles are aa; at q = 0.1, only 1 in 100, while 18 in 100 are hidden Aa carriers. Selection can barely reach the allele.
options: Correct: selection against a recessive phenotype weakens as the allele becomes rare.
The share of aa offspring falls because q falls, not because beetles adapt to the procedure.
Every reddish beetle was removed in every generation; there are simply very few of them when q is low.
Mutation rates are far too low to offset selection like this, and they do not depend on q.

items.q: In population 2 at generation 8, q = 0.10, and the newly formed offspring are in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. What percentage of the a alleles in these offspring are carried by heterozygotes? Give a whole number.

why.correct: Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18, carrying one a each: 0.18 copies per beetle. aa = q² = 0.01, carrying two each: 0.02. Share in heterozygotes = 0.18 ÷ (0.18 + 0.02) × 100 = 90%.

items.q: If population 3 were kept the same way for another 100 generations, q would end up closest to which value?

why.correct: Each generation, gene flow replaces 10% of the breeders with beetles from a stock at q = 0.10, so the population's q moves a tenth of the way toward 0.10 every generation and settles there.
options: Correct: gene flow pulls q toward the frequency in the source.
Nothing removes allele a in population 3, and the incoming beetles carry it at 0.10.
q passes 0.25 near generation 10 and keeps falling.
q left 0.50 in the first generation of gene flow.

items.q: Which Hardy-Weinberg condition is not met in population 4, and which feature of its graph supports this?
options: A very large population; q rises and falls at random instead of trending.
No natural selection; q falls steadily because reddish beetles die more often.
No gene flow; q moves toward the frequency in another stock of beetles.
Random mating; q stays at 0.50 while the share of heterozygous beetles falls.

why.correct: With only 10 breeders (20 gene copies), chance sampling moves q up and down in steps of 0.05 (one gene copy), often by 0.1 or more between the points plotted: genetic drift.
options: Correct: random swings show drift in a small population.
q in population 4 does not fall steadily; it rises to 0.80 at one point.
No beetles were added to population 4, and q does not move toward a fixed value.
Nonrandom mating changes genotype proportions without moving q, but q in population 4 moves a lot.

items.q: In a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of individuals show a recessive trait. What percentage of the population is expected to be homozygous dominant? Give a whole number.

why.correct: q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Homozygous dominant = p² = 0.49, or 49%. (Heterozygotes are 2pq = 42%.)

items.q: A population of 800 frogs is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a gene with p = 0.7. How many frogs are expected to be heterozygous? Give a whole number.

A student predicts that because allele B for brown fur is dominant, its frequency in a large, randomly mating mouse population with no selection will rise each generation until most mice are brown. Which response is correct?
options: Dominance sets which phenotype heterozygotes show; with no force acting, B's frequency stays constant.
The student is right, because heterozygotes look brown and so pass on the B allele more often than b.
The student is right, provided the starting frequency of B in the population is greater than 0.5.
The frequency of B will fall, because recessive alleles are hidden from selection in heterozygotes.

why.correct: Heterozygotes pass B and b to equal shares of their gametes, whatever they look like. Without drift, selection, gene flow, mutation or nonrandom mating, p and q stay the same in every generation.
options: Correct: this was Hardy's point in 1908.
A heterozygote's appearance does not change which alleles go into its gametes: half carry B, half b.
The starting frequency does not matter; with no force acting, any frequency stays put.
The stem says there is no selection, so hiding from selection has no effect here; the frequency stays constant.

items.q: Which of these are conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium? Select ALL that apply.
options: Mating is random with respect to genotype.
The population is very large.
No alleles enter or leave the population by gene flow.
Each genotype is present in equal numbers.
The dominant allele has a frequency above 0.5.
The alleles of the gene are codominant.

why.correct: The five conditions are random mating, a very large population, no gene flow, no net mutation and no natural selection. Genotype numbers, which allele is more common and the type of dominance are not conditions.
options: A condition: nonrandom mating changes genotype proportions.
A condition: a very large population makes drift negligible.
A condition: gene flow changes allele frequencies.
Not a condition: at equilibrium genotypes are at p², 2pq and q², which are equal only in special cases.
Not a condition: equilibrium holds at any allele frequency.
Not a condition: dominance does not affect allele or genotype frequencies.

items.q: Researchers compare observed genotype counts in a lizard population with Hardy-Weinberg expectations and get χ² = 12.4, well above the critical value at p = 0.05. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The population departs from equilibrium, so a condition fails; these data alone do not show which.
The population is evolving by natural selection, because a large χ² shows that one genotype is fitter.
The population is in equilibrium, because a large χ² means the observed counts fit the expected counts well.
The allele frequencies were probably calculated wrongly, because real populations do not differ this much.

why.correct: A large χ² means the difference is too big to blame on chance, so the null hypothesis of equilibrium is rejected. Selection, nonrandom mating, gene flow and drift can all cause departures; other evidence is needed to tell them apart.
options: Correct: reject equilibrium; identifying the cause needs more evidence.
Selection is one possibility, but nonrandom mating or gene flow could produce the same result.
A large χ² means a poor fit, not a good one.
Real populations often depart from equilibrium; that is why the test is useful.

items.q: A large plant population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with q = 0.2. A change in its pollinators makes the plants start fertilizing themselves, with no selection, drift, gene flow or mutation. Predict the change in each of these over the next few generations.

variables.name: Frequency of allele a (q)
variables.why: Self-fertilization pairs alleles differently but each plant still passes on its own alleles in the same proportions, so q stays 0.2.

variables.name: Proportion of heterozygous (Aa) plants
variables.why: A selfed Aa plant gives only half Aa offspring; AA and aa plants give only homozygotes, so heterozygotes fall each generation.

variables.name: Proportion of aa plants
variables.why: Selfed Aa plants produce aa offspring a quarter of the time and aa plants produce only aa, so aa rises above q² = 0.04.

why.correct: Nonrandom mating changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies: the population departs from p², 2pq, q² without its gene pool changing.

items.q: No real population meets all five Hardy-Weinberg conditions. Why are the equations still useful to biologists?
options: They predict what no evolution looks like, so a departure shows a process is acting and hints at which.
They predict the exact allele frequencies a population will have after several generations of selection.
They show that real populations do not evolve, because genotype frequencies in any population add up to 1.
They give the frequencies populations move toward over time, whatever processes act on them.

why.correct: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a null model. Comparing data with it tests whether a population is evolving or mating nonrandomly, as a control does in an experiment.
options: Correct: a baseline for detecting change.
The equations describe no change; predicting the effect of selection needs fitness values as well.
Genotype frequencies add up to 1 in any population, evolving or not.
Populations under selection, drift or gene flow move away from their starting frequencies, not toward a fixed set of them.

items.q: In a malaria region, newborns have sickle-cell genotypes that fit Hardy-Weinberg expectations, but a sample of adults from the same population has more heterozygotes than 2pq predicts. Which conclusion best fits these two observations?
options: Mating is random, but selection between birth and adulthood favors heterozygotes.
Mating is nonrandom, because adults choose partners with a different genotype from their own.
Drift has changed the allele frequencies between birth and adulthood, adding heterozygotes.
Gene flow brings heterozygous adults into the population, but no heterozygous newborns.

why.correct: Newborns at equilibrium show that gametes combine at random. The surplus of heterozygotes appears later, so it comes from survival: heterozygotes survive malaria better, and homozygotes for the sickle-cell allele often die young.
options: Correct: random mating at birth, selection during life.
If mating were nonrandom, newborns would already depart from expectations.
Drift changes allele frequencies by chance, in no set direction; it would not reliably produce a surplus of heterozygotes among adults.
Nothing suggests migrants, and gene flow would not add only heterozygotes.

items.q: Which observation provides the best evidence that a population is NOT evolving at a particular gene?
options: Over five generations, q stays near 0.30 and genotype counts fit p², 2pq and q².
In one year's sample, genotype counts fit p², 2pq and q² with a small χ² value.
The dominant phenotype is more common than the recessive one in each of the years sampled.
The frequencies of the three genotypes add up to 1 in each year sampled.

why.correct: Evolution is change across generations. Stable allele frequencies over several generations, with genotype counts matching expectations, is the strongest evidence of equilibrium.
options: Correct: stability over generations plus a good fit.
One sample can fit the equations even while allele frequencies are changing between generations.
A dominant phenotype is common at many allele frequencies, and says nothing about change.
Genotype frequencies add up to 1 in every population, so this is no evidence at all.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the expected number of heterozygotes from genotype counts in order.
options: Count the copies of allele A: 2 × (number of AA) + (number of Aa).
Divide by 2 × the total number of individuals to get p.
Find q from q = 1 − p.
Calculate the expected frequency of heterozygotes, 2pq.
Multiply 2pq by the number of individuals.

why.correct: Allele frequencies come from counting alleles; genotype expectations follow from p and q; multiplying by the sample size gives expected counts to compare with observed.
